inputs.system:
You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Science and Technology for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course.

Course: "10. Tissues and Its Types" · subject: Science and Technology · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.
Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the book's own terms and spellings.

Navin's rules for this section (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never shorten work to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, completeness wins.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type (definition, fact, process, structure, comparison, classification, timeline, cause_effect, formula, data, example, question). The content type decides later how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.

How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part) with a reason each, and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "".
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the list given.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree).
  - content_type: what the content really is (definition, fact, process, structure, comparison, classification, timeline, cause_effect,
    formula, data, example, question, other).
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (see S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside". BIE's code checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how"; a process needs "how"; a comparison or classification needs "compare" or
    "difference".
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

output.page_summary: Sclerenchyma occurs around vascular bundles, in leaf veins and in hard seed and nut coverings; its elongated, dead, closely packed cells have heavily lignified walls and provide protection and mechanical strength. Complex permanent tissues contain different cooperating cell types and transport water, minerals and food. Their two types are xylem and phloem. Xylem contains tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres, with roles in vertical conduction, food storage, sideways conduction and support. Two figures show these components and additional phloem structures, including sieve tubes, companion cells, sieve plates and plasmodesmata.

items.content: 3. Sclerenchyma Tissue
items.exam_note: Introduces an important plant tissue for structure–function and identification questions.

items.content: Occurrence:
items.exam_note: Organises the locations that follow.

items.content: • In stems around vascular bundles.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is sclerenchyma located in stems?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs around vascular bundles, placing the strengthening tissue near the stem's conducting tissues.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a strengthening tissue useful around vascular bundles?
teacher_understanding.answer: Rigid tissue around a conducting bundle helps reinforce the stem and protects the conducting region against mechanical deformation.

prerequisites: vascular bundle as a group of conducting tissues
items.exam_note: Learn the precise location: around vascular bundles in stems.

items.content: • In veins of leaves.

teacher_understanding.question: Which part of a leaf contains sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page identifies the veins of leaves as a site of sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How does sclerenchyma in a leaf vein help the leaf?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its thick, rigid walls help reinforce the vein and support the leaf blade around its conducting network.

items.exam_note: A standard location-based identification fact.

items.content: • Hard covering of seeds and nuts.

teacher_understanding.question: What hard plant coverings contain sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: The hard coverings of seeds and nuts contain sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is sclerenchyma suitable for a protective covering?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its heavily thickened walls resist mechanical damage and make a covering hard and protective.

items.exam_note: Connect hardness and protection with sclerenchyma rather than soft storage tissue.

items.content: Eg. Husk of coconut.

teacher_understanding.question: Which familiar example of sclerenchyma is supplied?
teacher_understanding.answer: The husk of coconut is the example.

teacher_understanding.question: How does coconut husk illustrate sclerenchyma's properties?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its tough fibres illustrate how thick-walled sclerenchyma can provide mechanical strength and protection.

items.exam_note: A frequently useful tissue–example match; retain 'husk', not a different coconut part.

items.content: Structure:
items.exam_note: Introduces sclerenchyma's structural features.

items.content:  Long and narrow

teacher_understanding.question: What cell shape does the page associate with sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes the cells as long and narrow.

teacher_understanding.question: How does an elongated shape assist support?
teacher_understanding.answer: Elongated supporting cells can run along a plant part and reinforce it over a length. This description is particularly characteristic of sclerenchyma fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: Does this shape describe every form of sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Standard classification also includes sclereids, which can be short or irregularly shaped; the page gives the elongated description without discussing those forms.

items.exam_note: Recognise the page's elongated-cell description without assuming all sclerenchyma cells have the same shape.

items.content:  Walls are thickened by LIGNINS

teacher_understanding.question: What substance thickens sclerenchyma walls?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page names LIGNINS as the wall-thickening material.

teacher_understanding.question: How does lignification contribute to mechanical strength?
teacher_understanding.answer: Lignin is deposited in the cell wall, making it more rigid and resistant to deformation. A thick lignified wall can provide support even after the living cell contents are lost.

items.exam_note: Lignified thick walls are a key diagnostic feature.

items.content:  Cell cavity is absent due to excessive thickness.

teacher_understanding.question: What relationship does the book state between wall thickness and the cell cavity?
teacher_understanding.answer: It states that excessive wall thickness makes the cell cavity absent.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a teacher explain wall thickening and the cavity accurately?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cavity inside a cell is its lumen. As wall material is deposited inward, the lumen becomes smaller. Sclerenchyma commonly retains a very narrow lumen, so the page's word 'absent' should not be presented as a universal anatomical rule.

items.exam_note: Understand the thick-wall/narrow-lumen relationship; the page's absolute wording needs qualification.

items.content:  Intercellular spaces absent.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the page say about spaces between sclerenchyma cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: It states that intercellular spaces are absent.

teacher_understanding.question: How is an intercellular space different from a cell cavity?
teacher_understanding.answer: An intercellular space lies between neighbouring cells; the cell cavity or lumen lies inside a cell wall. Close packing concerns spaces between cells, whereas wall thickening reduces the internal lumen.

items.exam_note: Do not confuse the absence of intercellular spaces with the size of the internal cell lumen.

items.content:  Cells are dead.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the living status of sclerenchyma cells as described here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page describes sclerenchyma cells as dead.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a dead cell still contribute to a plant?
teacher_understanding.answer: At maturity, the living contents can be lost while the thick lignified wall remains. Mechanical support depends on that wall, not on continued metabolic activity inside the cell.

items.exam_note: Dead at maturity is a major identification and comparison feature.

items.content: Function:
items.exam_note: Introduces sclerenchyma's functions.

items.content: • Provide strength to plant cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What strengthening role is stated for sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page says it provides strength to the plant cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How does sclerenchyma provide this strength?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its thick lignified walls resist bending and deformation, helping reinforce the plant part in which the cells occur.

items.exam_note: Link the function to wall properties rather than to living cell contents.

items.content: • Provides protection and mechanical strength

teacher_understanding.question: Which two functions are paired here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protection and mechanical strength are paired as functions of sclerenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the listed locations illustrate both functions?
teacher_understanding.answer: In stems and leaf veins, rigid walls reinforce the plant part. In seed and nut coverings, similar wall rigidity also creates a protective barrier against physical damage.

items.exam_note: Useful for matching tissue locations with support and protection.

items.content: COMPLEX PERMANENT TISSUE
items.exam_note: Begins the conducting-tissue section.

items.where_on_page: middle left, first point under complex permanent tissue
items.content: • Made up of more than one type of cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What makes a permanent tissue complex?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is made up of more than one type of cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How does complex tissue differ from simple permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Complex permanent tissue contains different cell types, whereas simple permanent tissue is made of one principal kind of cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can different cell types still count as one tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their identity as a tissue comes from coordinated performance of a common function, not from requiring identical cells.

items.exam_note: A central definition for distinguishing simple and complex tissues.

items.content: • Cells co-ordinate to perform common function.

teacher_understanding.question: What unites the different cells of complex permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: They coordinate to perform a common function.

teacher_understanding.question: How does xylem illustrate coordinated work by unlike cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids and vessels conduct water and minerals vertically, parenchyma stores food and helps sideways water conduction, and fibres provide support. These are complementary contributions within xylem.

prerequisites: division of labour within a tissue
items.exam_note: Complex tissue is coordinated organisation, not merely a mixture of cells.

items.content: Functions:
items.exam_note: Introduces transport functions.

items.content: • Transport water, minerals and food materials.

teacher_understanding.question: What materials do complex permanent tissues transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: They transport water, minerals and food materials.

teacher_understanding.question: How are these transport roles divided between the two complex tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem mainly transports water and dissolved minerals, while phloem transports organic food materials. The statement describes the combined transport roles of the two tissues, not an identical role for each.

items.exam_note: Do not assign food transport to xylem simply because all materials occur in this collective statement.

items.where_on_page: middle left, above lower boxed figure
items.content:
Two types:
1. Xylem
2. Phloem

teacher_understanding.question: What are the two types of complex permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem and phloem are the two types.

teacher_understanding.question: What classification do xylem and phloem share?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both belong to complex permanent tissue, whose different cell types coordinate to carry out common functions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it useful to separate them as two tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: They have different cellular arrangements and major transported materials: xylem is associated with water and mineral conduction, and phloem with food transport.

items.exam_note: Foundational classification and odd-one-out knowledge.

items.content: Figure headed 'Complex Permanent Tissue' places Xylem on the left and Phloem on the right. The green xylem drawing groups elongated conducting and supporting cells, with leader arrows to Xylem Parenchyma, Vessels, Tracheids and Xylem Fibres. The phloem drawing places broad, end-to-end sieve-tube cells beside narrower cells, with leader arrows to Phloem Parenchyma, Companion cell, Phloem fibres and Sieve tube. 'Xylem' and 'Phloem' appear beneath the respective drawings. The arrows identify parts; they do not indicate transport direction.

teacher_understanding.question: What does this figure show about complex permanent tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each tissue is drawn as a group of visibly different cell components: four labelled components in the xylem drawing and four in the phloem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a student read the arrows?
teacher_understanding.answer: Follow each leader from the cell or structure to its printed name. These are identification arrows, not a flow diagram showing movement of water or food.

teacher_understanding.question: What structural contrast can be recognised between the drawings?
teacher_understanding.answer: The xylem drawing labels vessels and tracheids, whereas the phloem drawing labels a sieve tube and companion cell. Both also label parenchyma and fibres.

items.exam_note: Use for visual component identification and xylem–phloem comparison.

items.content: Complex Permanent Tissue
items.exam_note: Title of the paired tissue figure.

items.where_on_page: middle-right figure, upper label beside xylem
items.content: Xylem Parenchyma — leader points to the narrow cellular region at the upper right of the xylem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which xylem component does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies xylem parenchyma, a component that stores food and helps sideways conduction of water.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this component extend xylem's role beyond vertical transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contributes storage and lateral movement, rather than serving mainly as the long vertical conducting tubes.

items.exam_note: Match parenchyma with storage and lateral conduction.

items.content: Vessels — leader points to the broad tubular component in the xylem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: What conducting component is labelled Vessels?
teacher_understanding.answer: The label identifies one of the tubular, thick-walled xylem components involved in vertical water and mineral transport.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a vessel suited to longitudinal conduction?
teacher_understanding.answer: Vessel elements join end to end, with perforations in their end walls providing a route for water through the vessel.

items.exam_note: Recognise a vessel as a conducting component, not a supporting fibre.

items.content: Tracheids — leader points to the elongated, tapering component toward the left of the xylem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Which component is identified by Tracheids?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids are one of the xylem components named here and are associated with vertical transport of water and minerals.

teacher_understanding.question: How does water move from one tracheid to another?
teacher_understanding.answer: It passes through pits in the walls between adjacent tracheids. Tracheids do not form the same perforated end-to-end vessel arrangement as vessel elements.

items.exam_note: Know tracheids as conducting cells and distinguish them from vessels.

items.content: Xylem Fibres — leader points to the narrow elongated supporting component in the xylem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the main role of the labelled xylem fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their main function is support.

teacher_understanding.question: How do fibres support the conducting tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their elongated form and thick lignified walls reinforce the tissue mechanically.

items.exam_note: Distinguish supportive fibres from the principal conducting elements.

items.where_on_page: beneath left half of middle-right figure
items.content: Xylem — names the left-hand group of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: Which of the paired drawings is xylem?
teacher_understanding.answer: The left drawing, containing the four labelled xylem components, is xylem.

teacher_understanding.question: How can its labels distinguish it from phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: Vessels and tracheids identify the xylem side; the other drawing instead labels a sieve tube and companion cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this group called a complex tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It combines several cell types rather than a single type.

items.exam_note: Identify xylem by its component combination.

items.content: Phloem Parenchyma — leader points to the small green cells along the outer right side of the phloem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: What component of phloem is identified here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The label identifies phloem parenchyma.

teacher_understanding.question: How does phloem parenchyma contribute to the tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: These living parenchyma cells participate in storage and lateral movement of organic materials within the phloem region.

items.exam_note: Recognise that parenchyma is named in both xylem and phloem.

items.content: Companion cell — leader points to the narrow green cell beside the broad sieve tube.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the companion cell shown?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is shown closely alongside a sieve tube in the phloem drawing.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this close association important?
teacher_understanding.answer: A mature sieve-tube element lacks a nucleus and depends on associated companion cells for metabolic support and assistance with sugar transport.

items.exam_note: Companion cell–sieve tube is a key structural and functional association.

items.content: Phloem fibres — leader points to the slender elongated supporting component beside the sieve tube.

teacher_understanding.question: Which phloem component is labelled as fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: The figure labels phloem fibres as a component of phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: How do phloem fibres contribute differently from sieve tubes?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem fibres are thick-walled supporting cells, whereas sieve tubes are the main food-conducting structures.

items.exam_note: Do not equate every phloem component with food conduction.

items.content: Sieve tube — leader points to the broad central tubular structure with perforated transverse end walls.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the Sieve tube label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the broad tube-like structure in the phloem drawing, with porous partitions between its successive sections.

teacher_understanding.question: How do those sections form a conducting pathway?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sieve-tube elements align end to end, and sieve-plate pores allow phloem sap to pass from one element to the next.

items.exam_note: Recognise the food-conducting tube and its porous end walls.

items.where_on_page: beneath right half of middle-right figure
items.content: Phloem — names the right-hand drawing containing phloem parenchyma, companion cell, phloem fibres and sieve tube.

teacher_understanding.question: Which group in this figure is phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: The right-hand group with the sieve tube and companion cell is phloem.

teacher_understanding.question: What named components distinguish it from the xylem drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sieve tube and companion cell occur as labels on the phloem side, while vessels and tracheids label the xylem side.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this drawing illustrate complex permanent tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Several unlike cell components are grouped together as one tissue.

items.exam_note: Identify phloem from its component combination.

items.where_on_page: lower-middle left, boxed figure above xylem bullet points
items.content: Boxed figure compares 'Xylem structure' on the left with 'Phloem structure' on the right. Pink xylem views show an isolated vessel element with pitted walls, a group of elongated tracheids with pitted walls, and a composite arrangement labelled xylem parenchyma cell, vessel element and tracheid. Blue phloem views show sieve-tube elements with sieve plates and associated companion and phloem parenchyma cells; a nucleus is marked in the narrow associated cell. The right-hand phloem view additionally labels plasmodesmata. Leader lines identify structures, not flow directions. Small a./b. marks identify subfigures.

teacher_understanding.question: What is being compared in this boxed figure?
teacher_understanding.answer: The structural components of xylem and phloem are placed side by side, with separate and grouped views of their cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the structures be distinguished visually?
teacher_understanding.answer: The xylem side labels pitted walls, vessels and tracheids. The phloem side labels sieve plates, sieve-tube elements, companion cells and plasmodesmata.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should pitted walls and sieve plates not be treated as the same feature?
teacher_understanding.answer: Xylem pits are regions where the secondary wall is absent, permitting movement across the remaining wall. Sieve plates are porous end-wall regions connecting successive living sieve-tube elements.

items.exam_note: Supports diagram identification and comparison of conducting structures.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, title above left half
items.content: Xylem structure — names the pink left-hand set of cell drawings.
items.exam_note: Subheading for the xylem views.

items.content: vessel elements — leader points to the isolated elongated pink conducting cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What is identified in the far-left xylem view?
teacher_understanding.answer: The drawing is labelled vessel elements.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a vessel element related to a vessel?
teacher_understanding.answer: A vessel element is an individual cell; successive elements join end to end to form a vessel.

items.exam_note: Distinguish an individual vessel element from a complete vessel.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, beside far-left vessel element
items.content: pitted walls — leader points to the marked wall regions of the isolated vessel element.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are pitted walls labelled in this view?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are labelled on the wall of the isolated vessel element.

teacher_understanding.question: How do pits assist movement of water?
teacher_understanding.answer: Pits lack the thick secondary wall deposition found around them, allowing water to move across pit membranes between adjacent cells.

items.exam_note: Pits are associated with exchange across xylem cell walls.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, central-left group of narrow pink cells
items.content: tracheids — leader points to the grouped elongated narrow xylem cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Which cells are named in the narrow grouped xylem view?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are labelled tracheids.

teacher_understanding.question: How do tracheids combine conduction with reinforcement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their hollow interior and wall pits permit water movement, while their lignified walls also strengthen the tissue.

items.exam_note: Recognise narrow elongated tracheids in a diagram.

items.content: pitted walls — leader points to wall markings on the grouped tracheids.

teacher_understanding.question: Which second xylem component is shown with pitted walls?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids, as well as the vessel element, are shown with pitted walls.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are pits important where neighbouring tracheids overlap?
teacher_understanding.answer: They provide lower-resistance routes across adjacent walls so water can pass from one tracheid to another.

items.exam_note: Pitted walls are not exclusive to vessel elements.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, top of composite xylem view
items.content: xylem parenchyma cell — leader points to the narrow column of cells alongside the larger conducting elements.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the labelled cellular column beside the conducting elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is labelled xylem parenchyma cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How does its role differ from that of a vessel element?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page assigns storage and sideways water conduction to parenchyma, while vessels participate in vertical water and mineral conduction.

items.exam_note: Match this component with storage and lateral conduction.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, upper label in composite xylem view
items.content: vessel element — leader points to the broad pink tubular cell in the composite xylem view.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the vessel element shown in the composite view?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is shown among the other xylem cells as the broader tubular component.

teacher_understanding.question: How does seeing it beside other cells clarify xylem organisation?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows that the conducting vessel component is part of a tissue containing different cell types, not the whole of xylem by itself.

items.exam_note: A vessel is a component of xylem, not a synonym for the entire tissue.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, beneath composite xylem view
items.content: tracheid — leader points to a narrow elongated cell alongside the vessel element.

teacher_understanding.question: Which conducting cell is labelled beside the vessel element?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tracheid is labelled beside it.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a tracheid differ structurally from a vessel element?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tracheid is generally elongated with tapering ends and conducts between cells through pits; vessel elements join through perforated end walls into vessels.

items.exam_note: A useful vessel-element versus tracheid comparison.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, title above right half
items.content: Phloem structure — names the blue right-hand set of cell drawings.
items.exam_note: Subheading for the phloem views.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, top label of left phloem view
items.content: sieve plate — leader points to the end-wall region at the upper end of the blue sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the sieve plate located in this view?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is labelled at the end of the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a sieve plate enable transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its pores permit phloem sap to pass between successive sieve-tube elements while an end-wall structure remains.

items.exam_note: Identify sieve plates as connections between successive sieve-tube elements.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, left side of left phloem view
items.content: sieve-tube element — leader points to the elongated blue conducting cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the blue conducting cell labelled here?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a sieve-tube element related to a sieve tube?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is one cell in a longitudinal series; the connected series forms the sieve tube.

items.exam_note: Distinguish an individual element from the complete conducting tube.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, left side of left phloem view, below sieve-tube label
items.content: companion cell — leader points to the narrow cell closely associated with the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the companion cell's position relative to the sieve-tube element?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies alongside the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a companion cell assist a sieve-tube element?
teacher_understanding.answer: It provides metabolic support and helps regulate the loading or unloading of sugars associated with phloem transport.

items.exam_note: Retain the close association of these two cell types.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, right side of left phloem view
items.content: nucleus — leader points to the dark oval in the narrow cell associated with the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: What organelle is marked by the nucleus label?
teacher_understanding.answer: The dark oval in the narrow associated cell is identified as the nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the nucleus important when discussing companion cells and sieve-tube elements?
teacher_understanding.answer: Companion cells retain a nucleus, whereas mature sieve-tube elements lack one. The nucleated companion cell helps maintain the functioning of its associated sieve-tube element.

items.exam_note: Useful for questions on living cells without a nucleus and their supporting cells.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, lower-left label beside left phloem view
items.content: phloem parenchyma cells — label identifies the parenchyma component associated with the left phloem view.

teacher_understanding.question: Which additional cell type is labelled in this phloem view?
teacher_understanding.answer: Phloem parenchyma cells are named in addition to the sieve-tube element and companion cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these cells contribute to phloem?
teacher_understanding.answer: They provide storage and participate in movement of organic materials across the tissue.

items.exam_note: Recognise parenchyma as a distinct phloem component.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, above right phloem view
items.content: companion cell — leader points to the narrow cell alongside the sieve-tube element in the right phloem view.

teacher_understanding.question: Which associated cell is labelled again in the right-hand phloem view?
teacher_understanding.answer: The companion cell is labelled again beside the sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should it not be mistaken for another sieve-tube element?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a distinct, narrower cell type with a retained nucleus and a metabolic-support role, rather than a segment of the main sieve tube.

items.exam_note: Identify the neighbouring support cell in a composite diagram.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, upper-right label beside right phloem view
items.content: sieve-tube element — leader points to a broad blue longitudinal conducting cell.

teacher_understanding.question: Which broad cell is labelled in the composite phloem view?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is labelled sieve-tube element.

teacher_understanding.question: How does its position in the series support food transport?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its end-to-end connection with other elements creates a continuous route for phloem sap through sieve-plate pores.

items.exam_note: Identify the main conducting cell in the grouped view.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, middle-right label beside right phloem view
items.content: sieve plate — leader points to a transverse junction between successive sieve-tube elements.

teacher_understanding.question: What junction is identified as a sieve plate?
teacher_understanding.answer: The transverse junction between successive sieve-tube elements is labelled sieve plate.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this label explain the tube's continuity?
teacher_understanding.answer: The sieve plate contains pores through which sap can pass across the boundary between neighbouring elements.

items.exam_note: Locate sieve plates at element junctions, not on an unrelated supporting cell.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, bottom-left label beneath right phloem view
items.content: phloem parenchyma cells — leader points to the associated cellular column at the side of the composite phloem view.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the side column identified by this label?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is identified as phloem parenchyma cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this label reinforce the meaning of complex tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It adds another distinct cell type to the sieve-tube and companion-cell components shown together in the tissue.

items.exam_note: Recognise the mixed cellular composition of phloem.

items.where_on_page: boxed figure, bottom-right label beneath right phloem view
items.content: plasmodesmata — printed across two lines as 'plasmo-' and 'desmata'; leader points to connections across the walls between adjacent phloem cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What intercellular connections are labelled in the right phloem view?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are labelled plasmodesmata.

teacher_understanding.question: How do plasmodesmata help adjacent living cells cooperate?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are cytoplasmic channels crossing cell walls, allowing communication and movement of substances between neighbouring living cells, including associated phloem cells.

teacher_understanding.question: How are plasmodesmata different from intercellular spaces?
teacher_understanding.answer: Plasmodesmata connect cell cytoplasm through walls; intercellular spaces are gaps between cells. They are not interchangeable terms.

items.exam_note: An image-only term useful for understanding cell-to-cell coordination.

items.where_on_page: bottom section, first bullet below boxed figure
items.content:  Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: What are the four components of xylem listed on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.

teacher_understanding.question: How do their principal roles compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tracheids and vessels conduct water and minerals vertically; xylem parenchyma stores food and helps sideways conduction of water; xylem fibres mainly support the tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this list demonstrate that xylem is complex?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contains several distinct cell types carrying out complementary tasks within one tissue.

items.exam_note: Memorise the complete component list and connect each component to its role.

items.content:  Tracheids and vessels have thick walls, and many are dead cells when mature.

teacher_understanding.question: Which structural and maturity features are stated for tracheids and vessels?
teacher_understanding.answer: They have thick walls, and the page says many are dead when mature.

teacher_understanding.question: How can dead conducting elements carry water?
teacher_understanding.answer: Loss of living contents leaves a hollow lumen through which water can move. The thick lignified walls help resist collapse under the tension associated with water transport.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the presence of dead conducting elements mean the whole xylem is dead?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Xylem is a mixed tissue; its parenchyma cells are generally living, even though mature tracheids and vessel elements are normally dead.

items.exam_note: Distinguish mature conducting elements from the living parenchyma component; preserve the book's wording 'many'.

items.where_on_page: bottom section, third bullet spanning two lines
items.content:  Tracheids and vessels are tubular structures. This allows them to transport water and minerals vertically.

teacher_understanding.question: What structure–function link does the page make for tracheids and vessels?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their tubular form enables vertical transport of water and minerals.

teacher_understanding.question: How does tubular organisation make long-distance transport possible?
teacher_understanding.answer: Elongated lumens provide longitudinal pathways. Vessel elements connect through perforated end walls, while tracheids transfer water between adjoining cells through pits.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is tube shape alone not a complete explanation of upward water movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tube shape supplies a pathway but does not itself supply the driving force. Transpiration from leaves helps generate tension that pulls water through xylem; cohesion helps maintain the water column.

items.exam_note: Link conducting-cell shape with vertical water and mineral movement; do not confuse pathway with driving force.

items.content:  The parenchyma stores food and help in sideways conduction of water.

teacher_understanding.question: What two functions are assigned to xylem parenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stores food and helps in sideways conduction of water.

teacher_understanding.question: How does sideways conduction differ from the conduction described for tracheids and vessels?
teacher_understanding.answer: Sideways conduction moves water laterally across tissue, whereas the page associates tracheids and vessels with vertical movement along the plant.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does food storage in xylem not mean xylem is the main food-transport tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Storage is retaining material within cells; transport is moving it between regions. Xylem parenchyma can store food while phloem remains the principal tissue for transporting organic food materials.

items.exam_note: Food storage and lateral water conduction are distinguishing functions of xylem parenchyma.

items.content:  Xylem fibres are mainly supportive in function.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the main function of xylem fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their main function is support.

teacher_understanding.question: How do xylem fibres provide support?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are elongated, thick-walled sclerenchymatous cells whose lignified walls mechanically reinforce xylem and the surrounding plant part.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this role compare with those of other xylem components?
teacher_understanding.answer: Fibres mainly support; tracheids and vessels conduct vertically; parenchyma stores food and helps lateral water conduction.

items.exam_note: Complete the xylem component–function matching set with fibres → support.
